 Valid: Nov 25 - 29, 2026 (6-10 Day Outlook) Valid: Nov 27 - Dec 03, 2026 (8-14 Day Outlook) Issued: Nov 19, 2026
Prognostic Discussion for 6 to 10 and 8 to 14 Day Outlooks
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
3:00 PM EST Thu November 19 2026
6-10 Day Outlook for Wed Nov 25 2026 - Sun Nov 29 2026
The 0Z European ensemble (ECENS) mean, 0z and 6z GEFS mean, and 0z Canadian
ensemble (CMCE) mean are in fairly good agreement on the mean large-scale
circulation pattern over the North American domain during the 6-10 day period.
There are differences in the details, however, that introduce some uncertainty.
Models forecast a mean 500-hPa trough over the southeastern Contiguous States
(CONUS) with a positive height anomaly centered to the north over east-central
Canada. Mid-level ridging extends weakly from Canada into the Southwest while a
broad and fairly strong upstream trough is centered south of the Gulf of Alaska.
Overall the GEFS mean is more amplified with this trough than the CMCE and ECENS
means, which is more consistent with yesterday’s models, but all three
ensemble means show a weaker feature than yesterday, continuing the trend of the
guidance the last couple of days. The forecast pattern is a compromise of the
ensemble means and the dynamical European (ECMWF) leaning toward the GEFS due to
its better consistency with yesterday’s solutions. To the east, the mid-level
ridging in central Canada is also a bit weaker than yesterday, especially in the
ECENS mean, while the mean mid-level trough centered over the southeastern CONUS
is similar to yesterday’s solutions in all of the ensemble means.
The southeastern CONUS trough is expected to trigger surface low pressure
development near the southern Atlantic Seaboard. One storm system is expected to
ride northward along or near the Eastern Seaboard early in the period, with a
secondary system potentially taking a similar path late in the period. Although
surface low pressure development seems likely, there is a great deal of
uncertainty regarding how close to the coast any storm system tracks and thus
how far inland significant precipitation will reach. This is especially true
over the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Models have not been consistent in handling
the development and track of storm systems, and the individual members of the
ensembles depict solutions ranging from a track just east of the Appalachians to
one well east of the coast. Given the position and evolution of the mid-level
trough, a track closer to or possibly just inland along the East Coast is
favored, though not with a lot of confidence. Meanwhile, mid-level troughing is
expected early in the period to the west or northwest of Hawaii which lifts
northward with time, resulting in rising 500-hPa heights. And to the north,
despite the presence of a strong mid-level trough in the North Pacific,
generally near- to somewhat above-normal 500-hPa heights are expected across
Alaska, with the greatest positive height departures near the northern part of
the state.
Above normal temperatures are favored from portions of the Great Lakes and
northern Great Plains westward and southwestward to cover areas from the Rockies
to the Pacific Coast. The best chances for above-normal temperatures (over 60
percent) cover the immediate West Coast (consistent with most temperature tools)
and the extreme north-central CONUS (near the greatest mean positive height
anomalies). Meanwhile, an intrusion of cooler than normal air is expected near
and just upstream from the mid-level trough over the Southeast, reaching as far
north as the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers’ confluence. Odds for subnormal
temperatures exceed 50 percent from portions of the Lower Mississippi Valley
westward through much of central and eastern Texas. Temperatures should average
closer to normal along most of the East Coast and over the middle and upper Ohio
Valley. Alaska is expected to average warmer than normal under above-normal
 500-hPa heights, especially in eastern portions of the state. Cooler than normal
mean temperatures are anticipated over central and northwestern Hawaii, although
conditions are expected to moderate late in the period beneath rising 500-hPa
heights and under the influence of adjacent above-normal sea surface
temperatures.
The positioning and strength of cyclonic flow over the northeastern Pacific,
downstream from the amplified mid-level trough, is expected to promote a fairly
active weather pattern along the West Coast. Above normal precipitation is
expected, with the best chances (over 50 percent) extending along the Pacific
Coast from central California northward to the Canadian border. Meanwhile, the
downstream mid-level trough over the Southeast is expected to spin up one or
possibly two surface low pressure systems that will likely affect at least
portions of the East Coast. Chances for above-normal precipitation exceed 50
percent from the Florida Peninsula along the immediate Atlantic Coast from
Georgia through the Carolinas. Odds for heavy precipitation decrease to the
north and west due to uncertainty regarding the track of any low pressure system
that develops, and thus how far inland significant precipitation will reach.
Subnormal precipitation is favored in and near southern Arizona, and from
portions of the Middle Mississippi Valley northward through the northern Great
Plains, Upper Mississippi Valley, and Upper Great Lakes. This is consistent with
the consolidation and with precipitation forecasts derived from the favored GEFS
mean. Farther north, above-normal precipitation is nominally favored over the
southeastern Alaska Mainland and the Panhandle while drier than normal
conditions are expected over western and northern parts of the Mainland.
Subnormal rainfall is also anticipated over northwestern Hawaii, consistent with
GEFS reforecast output.
The official 6-10 day 500-hPa height blend consists of 25% of Today's 0z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 25% of Today's 6z GFS Ensemble Mean centered on
Day 8, 20% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 15% of
Today's operational 0z ECMWF centered on Day 8, and 15% of Today's 0z Canadian
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8
Forecast Confidence for the 6-10 Day Period: Above average, 4 out of 5, due to
fairly good agreement among today's model height solutions, offset by
differences in the amplitudes of individual features, uncertainty regarding
storm development along the East Coast, and differences between raw and
reforecast temperature and precipitation output from the ensembles.
8-14 Day Outlook for Fri Nov 27 2026 - Thu Dec 03 2026
The latest ECENS, CMCE, and GEFS means show similar forecast patterns for
week-2, but there is uncertainty regarding the exact placement and amplitude of
individual features. This is particularly true of the amplified 500-hPa trough
in the North Pacific. This feature broadens relative to the 6- to 10-day period,
with the negative 500-hPa height anomaly center retrograding, resulting in a
mean position farther west than models depicted yesterday. The 6z GEFS depicts
the greatest negative height anomalies south of the eastern Aleutians while the
0z CMCE mean pulls the trough much farther northwest, with the axis of lowest
 500-hPa heights stretching from the westernmost Aleutians into Siberia. The
ECENS mean approximately splits the difference. The forecast leans toward the
GEFS mean, which is most consistent with yesterday’s models, but not with
great confidence since most other guidance places the system farther west.
Across North America, models are in better agreement, keeping positive height
 anomalies in place from Alaska through Canada, with the greatest positive
 anomalies near or just south of Hudson Bay. Farther south, after a mid-level
shortwave and an associated surface low pressure system exits the eastern CONUS
and weakens, the 500-hPa trough over the Southeast reloads, resulting in a mean
position and amplitude similar to the 6- to 10-day period. Meanwhile, the
ensemble means are in good agreement forecasting increasing 500-hPa heights as a
broad, flat ridge forms near the central Pacific, resulting in mean height
 anomalies of 4 to 7 dm across a large part of the lower North Pacific, including
Hawaii.
Above normal temperatures are favored across a majority of the CONUS, with near-
or below-normal temperature forecasts restricted to the southern Great Plains,
Lower Mississippi Valley, and the Southeast. The best chances for abnormal
warmth cover the northernmost western Great Lakes and part of northern
Minnesota, where odds exceed 70 percent closest to the positive 500-hPa
 anomalies centered over Canada. Chances for above-normal temperatures top 50
percent over the Pacific Coast States and the northern tier of the CONUS from
the Rockies through the Great Lakes. There is substantial uncertainty in the
temperature forecast farther south. Raw ensemble output favors subnormal
temperatures over a large part of the south-central and southeastern CONUS while
the reforecasts favor near- or slightly above-normal temperatures, with the
ECENS reforecast being particularly bullish. The official forecast is a
compromise, nominally favoring subnormal mean temperatures from eastern Texas
through the central Gulf Coast States and across southern Georgia. Abnormally
warm conditions are expected to continue across Alaska, especially in
southeastern sections, while increasing temperatures are expected across Hawaii
progressively from east to west under rising 500-hPa heights. Week-2
temperatures are favored to average above normal across the Big Island, below
normal in Kauai and Nihau, and near normal across the interior of the island
chain.
Wetter than normal weather is favored for week-2 across the western CONUS in
cyclonic flow downstream from the Pacific mid-level trough . Farther east,
above-normal precipitation is also favored from the southern Plains through the
Tennessee and Lower Mississippi Valleys, the Gulf Coast Region, and much of the
Eastern Seaboard in association with the persistent 500-hPa trough centered over
the south-central and southeastern CONUS . Chances for surplus precipitation
exceed 40 percent west of the Rockies and near the Gulf and South Atlantic
Coasts. Between these two areas, from the Southwest through much of the Plains
and most locations from the Ohio and Middle Mississippi River Valleys northward,
there is significant uncertainty. Raw and derived output from the ECENS and CMCE
tend to favor somewhat above-normal precipitation over much of this area while
 analogs and GEFS output depict drier solutions. The official forecast is a
compromise, favoring near-normal amounts. The small exception is over the Upper
Great Lakes, where tools are in better agreement favoring subnormal
precipitation. Across Alaska, wetter than normal conditions remain nominally
favored in southeastern areas while the northern and western tiers of the
Mainland are more likely to experience an unusually dry week-2. Subnormal
precipitation is also favored across Hawaii under building mid-level heights and
weak zonal flow.
The official 8-14 day 500-hPa height blend consists of 50% of Today's 6z GFS
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11, 20% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean
centered on Day 11, and 30% of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on Day
11
Forecast Confidence for the 8-14 Day Period: About average, 3 out of 5, due to
increasing uncertainty in the prevailing mid-level pattern with time, and
inconsistent temperature and precipitation results from the ensembles.
Forecaster: Tinker

week 3-4.text:
Prognostic Discussion for Week 3-4 Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks
 NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
 300PM EST Fri Nov 13 2026
 Week 3-4 Forecast Discussion Valid Sat Nov 28 2026-Fri Dec 11 2026
 The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) Alert System Status is set to El Niño Advisory. Equatorial sea surface temperatures (SSTs) are above average across the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. The atmospheric circulation anomalies over the equatorial Pacific Ocean are consistent with El Niño. El Niño continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very-strong El Niño likely through January-March 2027 (remaining greater than an 83% chance).
 Realtime Multivariate (RMM) observations show a stationary Indian Ocean Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) event that has steadily grown in amplitude over phase 2 amid a very strong El Niño background state during the past week. Dynamical models favor a resumption of eastward propagating MJO activity during the next week, but vary significantly in regards to its progression and strength later in November. A focal point concerns how well models develop the ensuing lower-level westerly phase of the MJO over the Indian Ocean, as this presents the early stages of destructive interference with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole circulation, as well as with the strong El Niño. A reinforcement of the low frequency response is favored in the extended leads, which could point to continued MJO activity that resurfaces over the equatorial Pacific. Some RMM forecasts feature a fast propagation of the MJO signal, with a return to the western Pacific and/or Western Hemisphere, before the end of November. Despite these uncertainties in the dynamical RMM based MJO forecasts, enhanced (suppressed) convection is likely to persist over the equatorial Pacific (Maritime Continent). This is consistent with the ongoing El Niño. The MJO, along with other modes of tropical variability, will act to modulate these low frequency responses.
 An equally weighted blend of dynamical and statistical forecast tools feature anomalous troughing over the North Pacific Ocean and across the Southern Tier of the contiguous U.S. (CONUS), and anomalous ridging centered over Canada. The models are well aligned, but vary on the position and axis of the troughing and ridge. The ECMWF forecast the gradients between the trough and ridge further west, toward the Pacific Northwest, while the CFS forecast the gradients near the Central Plains. The GEFS and the JMA forecast the gradients more to the north, along the border between CONUS and Canada.
 The guidance broadly agrees on elevated chances for above average temperatures across Alaska, the West Coast, and the Northern Tier of CONUS, with the highest probabilities forecast by the ECMWF over the Northern Plains and Upper Great Lakes. Both the JMA and the ECMWF forecast elevated chances for below average temperatures across the Southwest, Southern Plains, and Southeast while the CFS and the GEFS maintain a modest tilt toward above average temperatures in the same areas. The statistical guidance also forecasts below average temperatures across the Southwest and Central Rockies. The temperature outlook reflects an equally weighted blend of dynamical and statistical forecast tools with an area of Equal Chances forecast where the forecast guidance is most uncertain.
 Dynamical and statistical guidance broadly agree on elevated chances for above average precipitation across the Southern Tier and up the Eastern Seaboard. The highest probabilities for above average precipitation is forecast along the North and South Carolina coast. Elevated chances for above normal precipitation are forecast across the South Coast and Panhandle of Alaska. Elevated chances for below average precipitation are forecast for the Northern Plains, Upper Mississippi Valley, and parts of the Upper Great Lakes region. The highest probabilities for below normal precipitation are forecast along the Montana and North Dakota border. Below normal precipitation is forecast for the North Slope and Western regions of Alaska.
 For Hawaii, the outlook favors above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation for all of the islands.
 Forecaster: Emerson LaJoie
 The next week 3-4 outlook will be issued on Friday, Nov 20, 2026
 These outlooks are based on departures from the 1991-2020 base period
 These are three category outlooks consistent with what is currently used for the monthly and seasonal forecasts.
 The shading on the temperature map depicts the most favored category, either above-normal (A), below-normal (B), or near-normal (N) with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 The shading on the precipitation map depicts the most favored category, either above-median (A), below-median (B), or near-median with the solid lines giving the probability ( >33%) of this more likely category (above, below, or near).
 In areas where the likelihoods of 2-week mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are similar to climatological probabilities, equal chances (EC) is indicated.

Prognostic Discussion for Monthly Outlook NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 300 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026 30-DAY OUTLOOK DISCUSSION FOR NOV 2026 The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are updated considering monthly Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2) temperature and precipitation forecasts, as well as information from an experimental monthly calibrated version of the Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFSv12), and information from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) model for the month of November. We also consider shorter term guidance and official Outlooks across the month, including days 1 to 7 precipitation, extended-range (6-10 Day and Week-2) tools and Outlooks, and subseasonal (Weeks 3-4) tools and Outlooks. The ongoing El Nino remains the dominant teleconnection to influence this forecast, overshadowing any potential impacts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) despite an amplifying MJO signal that recently progressed eastward over the Indian Ocean basin, and the potential for continued eastward propagation in dynamical model forecasts. Adding to the uncertainty of this forecast, model forecasts indicate the potential for a stratospheric polar vortex disruption and a possible transition into a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) next week. A November SSW is very rare, and should this occur, impacts can be seen for up to 2 months, usually manifesting as a negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) phase, which can already be seen in models. A negative AO is in contrast with the forecasted phase of the Pacific-North American (PNA) pattern, which is more in alignment with El Nino. These factors add some uncertainty to the eastern U.S., where some of the potential impacts of a SSW and negative AO compete with those from El Nino. Toward the early part of November, above-average heights are forecast across Canada and northern parts of the Contiguous United States (CONUS). Over the southern states, the pattern is more transient with weaker and progressive troughing forecast to move across the southern part of the CONUS. By mid-November, troughing off the West Coast is forecast to strengthen and move toward the coast, causing the ridging downstream to build and expand further southward and eastward. Late in the month, weeks 3-4 guidance favors persistence of the northern CONUS ridging. Troughing remains present off the West Coast of the US, and there is some potential for troughing to settle over the Southeast by the end of the month as well; however, models are uncertain on placement and strength. Overall, the beginning to middle of November is characterized by above average heights over the north, an active southern tier with progressive troughing, and below average heights to the west and east of the CONUS. By the end of November, the mid-level height pattern resembles a classic El Nino response. The pattern of strong troughing off the West Coast with ridging over Canada and northern parts of the CONUS leads to generally increasing 500 hPa height anomalies from south to north across Alaska by mid-to-late November, but the evolution becomes more uncertain as the month progresses. The updated November Temperature Outlook resembles the initial November Outlook in terms of the broad pattern of enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern CONUS and along both coasts. However, there are some key changes in the updated Temperature Outlook, including expansion of above-normal temperatures across the state of Alaska, increased coverage of above-normal temperatures over the CONUS, reaching further south and covering more of the Southeast, and expansion of 50 to 60% probabilities of above-normal temperatures across the northern tier. The persistent ridging forecast throughout the month of November supports the increased coverage and strengthening of probabilities over the northern tier. Monthly CFSv2 forecasts depict high probabilities (greater than 75%) across Alaska, the northern CONUS, and the Southeast. However, probabilities are weaker in shorter-term tools, the experimental GEFSv12 and ECMWF, and the potential for cooler periods linked to the SSW and negative AO warrant lower probabilities than CFSv2. Transient guidance over the southern tier increases uncertainty early in the month, and equal-chances of above-, near-, and below-normal (EC) temperatures are indicated where guidance diverges the most. The potential late-month Southeast CONUS troughing reduces probabilities there, however, monthly guidance still agrees on a tilt toward above-normal temperatures. The highest confidence (60 to 70% chances) is located over the Northern Plains and Upper Mississippi Valley, aligned with persistent ridging and strong model agreement. While the updated Precipitation Outlook favors above-normal precipitation in that region which may lead to some cooling, this precipitation is expected to fall early in November. Though there is some uncertainty over western parts of Alaska, the pattern and above-average SSTs to the south generally support above-normal temperatures for the month. Larger changes were made to the updated November Precipitation Outlook to account for the potential for early-November precipitation across parts of the Southwest, Central and Northern Plains, and Upper Mississippi Valley. Since these regions are generally dry, it is much easier for short-lived early November precipitation to tilt the Outlook for the month to above-normal. Days 1 to 7 QPF indicates upper-tercile accumulations across parts of the Southwest and the Central and Northern Plains. Supported by monthly CFSv2, GEFSv12, and ECMWF guidance, above-normal precipitation probabilities are raised to 60% in the Southwest, with a 50% tilt across the north-central CONUS. Troughing off the Northwest Coast also supports a tilt toward above-normal precipitation along much of the West, including the Pacific Northwest, however, timing and amount of precipitation is uncertain. Conversely, probabilities are decreased across the Southeast and East Coast relative to the initial November Outlook. Most tools for the initial November Outlook favored a largely El Nino driven response over the Southeast and East Coast. However, the transient pattern for at least the first half of November increases uncertainty for the Southeast, and early November QPF forecasts are quite dry for much of the East and Southeast (except over peninsular Florida). In addition, Week 2 precipitation forecasts favor a weak below-normal precipitation probability that covers parts of the East and dips into the Southeast, also increasing uncertainty. Some moderate probability for above-normal precipitation remains over the Southeast given monthly dynamical model forecasts, but probabilities are weaker than the initial Outlook. Over Alaska, dynamical models had more agreement than in the initial Outlook and are in agreement with a typical El Nino response over the State. ****************************************************************************** ***** Previous mid-month discussion below ***** ****************************************************************************** The November 2026 Monthly Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks are based on dynamical models, local sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, El Nino teleconnections, and decadal trends . Guidance incorporates individual models and multi-model ensembles (MME) from the Copernicus Climate System (C3S) and the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME), alongside probability anomaly correlation (PAC) calibrated NMME forecasts and statistical tools blending SSTs and trends . Short-term early November forecasts from the Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2), the Global Ensemble Forecast System version 12 (GEFSv12), and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) models are utilized, along with monthly forecasts from CFSv2 and the experimental beta version of the Seasonal Forecast System (SFS) model. El Nino is expected to be the dominant climate driver, overshadowing the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), though localized SST influences are possible. Dynamical model forecasts closely align with the expected El Nino teleconnection for November. However, short-term fluctuations in the pattern can occur, adding to uncertainty in some areas. Furthermore, while current El Nino conditions are forecast to strengthen, November can still be a transition month for ENSO impacts for some regions, with teleconnections strengthening through the winter months. The November 2026 Temperature Outlook depicts enhanced above-normal probabilities across the northern two-thirds of the Contiguous United States (CONUS) and along both coasts. Overall, models and tools favor a warmer northern tier of the CONUS, particularly over Washington and the interior Northwest, Northern Plains, Upper Mississippi Valley, and Great Lakes where probabilities are highest in the Outlook. Probabilities are damped over Oregon due to neutral SST anomalies . However, a southerly gradient toward above-average SSTs maintains a tilt toward above-normal along the West Coast. Probabilities are also weaker over Montana and North Dakota where diving troughs may introduce cooler spells. Inter-model spread increases uncertainty over New England and other areas where probabilities are comparatively lower. Equal chances (EC) of above-, near-, and below-normal temperatures are indicated over the Southwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley, including parts of the Central Plains and Intermountain West. While El Nino typically supports below-normal temperatures over the Southern Plains and Southwest, inconsistent model signals regarding the placement and strength of any below-normal temperatures prompt a tilt toward EC. For Alaska, enhanced probabilities transition from near-normal in the west to above-normal across the east, the southeast Mainland, and Southeast Alaska. Monthly models and tools and early November dynamical model forecasts are in very good agreement on above-normal temperatures over much of eastern Alaska, aligning with El Nino teleconnections, long-term temperature trends , and above-average coastal SSTs to the south. Western Alaska carries higher uncertainty, with most models showing weakening probabilities, EC, or isolated transitions toward below-normal temperatures. This results in an EC forecast for the remainder of the state, aside from a small NMME-based near-normal area on the west coast. The November 2026 Precipitation Outlook indicates enhanced above-normal probabilities across much of the southern US and the East Coast, with below-normal precipitation favored from the northern Intermountain West into parts of the Northern Plains, as well as parts of the Great Lakes. Model agreement is exceptionally high over the Southeast, with MMEs showing greater than 70% chances of above-normal precipitation in isolated areas. Accordingly, 60 to 70% probabilities are forecast for parts of the region. The above-normal precipitation extends up the East Coast, but increasing inter-model spread over New England supports a transition to EC. Similarly, disagreement regarding the northward extent of precipitation along the West Coast and central Plains results in EC designations, as location is difficult to pinpoint at this lead time amid high model spread . The western below-normal precipitation signal remains spatially consistent and aligns with El Nino, though some models expand it weakly toward the coast. However, uncertainty over the Pacific Northwest remains high enough to warrant EC along the coast. The eastern below-normal signal is most consistent over the Great Lakes, though some models like CFSv2 extend it further south toward the Gulf States. Over Alaska, a weak trend -based tilt toward below-normal precipitation covers the southwestern mainland and parts of the Aleutians, with elevated above-normal chances along the northern coast. EC is favored for the rest of the state due to weak, inconsistent model signals and November's status as an ENSO transition month before below-normal teleconnections become prevalent later in winter. FORECASTER: Johnna Infanti The climatic normals are based on conditions between 1991 and 2020, following the World Meteorological Organization convention of using the most recent 3 complete decades as the climate reference period.  The probability anomalies for temperature and precipitation based on these new normals better represent shorter term climatic anomalies than the forecasts based on older normals. Prognostic Discussion for Long-Lead Seasonal Outlooks NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD 830 AM EST Thu Nov 19 2026 SUMMARY OF THE OUTLOOK FOR NON-TECHNICAL USERS A strong El Nino continues and is forecast to persist through January-February-March 2027. The strong El Nino is likely to be the major influence on temperatures and precipitation this winter through next spring. The Temperature Outlook for December-January-February (DJF) 2026-2027 favors above-normal temperatures for central to eastern Alaska along with much of the northern two-thirds of the Contiguous U.S. (CONUS). Above-normal temperature probabilities exceed 50% across the Northeast, Great Lakes, Upper Mississippi Valley, Pacific Northwest, and southeastern Alaska. Near-normal temperatures, averaged over the three-month period, are favored for parts of the Southeast. The DJF Precipitation Outlook depicts an increased chance of above-normal precipitation for southwestern Oregon, California, the Southwest, Central to Southern Great Plains, Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and much of the Northeast. The largest above-normal precipitation probabilities (> 70% chance) are forecast across Florida, southern Georgia, and the coastal Carolinas. Below-normal precipitation is more likely for parts of the Great Lakes, Northern High Plains, Northern Rockies, and Mainland Alaska. Equal chances (EC, white areas) are forecast for areas where probabilities for each category (below, near, or above) of three-month mean temperatures and accumulated precipitation amounts are forecast to be similar to climatological probabilities. BASIS AND SUMMARY OF THE CURRENT LONG-LEAD OUTLOOKS Note: For Graphical Displays of the Forecast Tools Discussed Below See: http://www. cpc .ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/90day/tools/briefing CURRENT ATMOSPHERIC AND OCEANIC CONDITIONS As of mid-November, weekly observed sea surface temperature (SST) departures in the Nino 3.4 region are +2.2 degrees C with equatorial SSTs above average across the east-central Pacific Ocean. Upper-ocean (0 to 300 meters) anomalies from the Date Line to 100W are near +2.5 degrees C but have decreased slightly since peaking in September. The Relative Oceanic Nino Index for August-September-October was +2.0 degrees C, just shy of +2.1 degrees C in 1997. From mid-October to mid-November, below-average OLR anomalies (enhanced convection and precipitation) were observed across the east-central equatorial Pacific with above-average OLR anomalies (suppressed convection and precipitation) across Indonesia and the Maritime Continent. Low-level and upper-level (850-hPa and 200-hPa) wind anomalies were westerly and easterly, respectively, from 160E to 120W. The oceanic and atmospheric observations reflect an ongoing strong El Nino. Any Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) signal continues to be overwhelmed and masked by the strong El Nino. Upper-level velocity potential anomaly observations depict a MJO that propagated east to the Indian Ocean by mid-November. Dynamical model forecasts indicate that this MJO may propagate east to the Western Hemisphere by the beginning of December. However, the MJO is unlikely to have much influence on the mid-latitude circulation pattern given the strength of the El Nino. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF SST FORECASTS As of November 12, the NOAA outlook indicates that El Nino is likely to persist through MAM 2027 with a transition to ENSO-neutral conditions becoming more probable by AMJ. The SST consolidation forecast for Nino 3.4 depicts SST anomalies peaking above +2.5 degrees C during NDJ 2026-27 and decreasing later in the winter and into the spring. By the 2027 fall and 2027-28 winter, this prognostic tool depicts a weak to moderate La Nina with SST anomalies between -0.5 and -1.0 degrees C. PROGNOSTIC TOOLS USED FOR U.S. TEMPERATURE AND PRECIPITATION OUTLOOKS The Temperature and Precipitation Outlooks from DJF 2026-27 through AMJ 2027 were based on: dynamical models such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) and the International Multi-Model Ensemble (IMME) along with an objective, historical skill-weighted consolidation that includes the NMME along with statistical tools such as the SST-based Constructed Analog and the ENSO-OCN. Also, for DJF 2026-27, observed temperatures and precipitation during stronger El Ninos (since 1997-98) and strong/very strong El Nino composites were heavily weighed. Beginning in MJJ and through OND 2027, ENSO-OCN (combination of ENSO and long-term trend) was the primary tool used. During NDJ and DJF 2027-28, the outlooks incorporated La Nina composites. PROGNOSTIC DISCUSSION OF OUTLOOKS - DJF 2026 TO DJF 2027 TEMPERATURE The historically strong El Nino is forecast to be the major influence on the mid-latitude circulation pattern and temperatures this winter. Typically during El Nino winters, DJF temperatures average above normal for most of the northern two-thirds of the CONUS with three-month temperatures more variable and averaging either below, near, or above normal for the southern third of the CONUS. The DJF 2026-27 outlook closely followed El Nino composites and the latest dynamical model output (NMME and IMME). Above-normal temperature probabilities exceed 50% for much of the Northeast, Great Lakes, Upper Mississippi Valley, Pacific Northwest, and southeastern Alaska. In addition, these probabilities are largest (> 60%) from northwestern Oregon and Washington northward to southeastern Alaska due to the latest dynamical model output and strong/very strong El Nino composites. Forecast uncertainty is higher for the Southwest, Southern Great Plains, Gulf Coast, and Southeast during the 2026-27 winter through the 2027 spring. Without a major shift in any of the model guidance, no changes were made to these areas from the previous outlook. In the more recent stronger El Ninos (2023-24, 2015-16, and 1997-98), temperatures varied largely over the Southwest where equal chances (EC) of below, near, or above-normal temperature are forecast. During the 2023-24 and 1997-98 winters, DJF temperatures verified in the middle tercile for most of Florida and from southeastern Louisiana east to southern Georgia. Therefore, the DJF 2026-27 temperature outlook leans towards near normal temperatures being the most likely outcome for that part of the Southeast. The DJF temperature observations for 2009-10 (stronger El Nino) was heavily influenced by a persistent and highly negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) with the following monthly values: Dec: -3.4, Jan: -2.6, Feb: -4.3. Although the 2009-10 winter outcome with a broad coverage of below-normal temperatures across the Great Plains and Southeast can not be completely ruled out, it is the least likely one among the more recent stronger El Ninos. The primary source of uncertainty in the temperature outlook is how much high latitude blocking prevails this winter. The AO and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) was in a positive phase from mid-September through October, but became negative in early November. The GEFS and ECMWF ensemble means favor a -NAO heading into December. A -NAO would tend to result in below-normal temperatures across the Southeast but there is high uncertainty on the NAO phase through the 2026-27 winter. El Nino impacts are expected to persist through at least the spring 2027 and the temperature outlooks reflect this. The outlooks from MJJ through OND 2027 are based primarily on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool which is derived from the CPC SST consolidation (ENSO component) and long term temperature trends (Optimal Climate Normal). Historically, La Nina follows a strong El Nino and given this likelihood, the NDJ and DJF 2027-28 outlooks were based more on typical La Nina influences. PRECIPITATION Due to the historically strong El Nino and its reliable wet pattern for a majority of the CONUS, there is higher forecast confidence in the precipitation than the temperature outlook this winter. For DJF 2026-27, a predicted active southern stream along with enhanced subtropical moisture leads to a large coverage of greater than a 40% chance of above-normal precipitation from southwestern Oregon and California east through the Southwest, Central to Southern Great Plains, Gulf Coast, and much of the East Coast. Based on the latest dynamical model output, above-normal precipitation probabilities were increased across California, the Desert Southwest, and along the East Coast compared to the previous forecast release on October 15. In southern California and southwestern Arizona, probabilities exceed 60% while greater than a 70% chance of above-normal precipitation is forecast for Florida, southern Georgia, and the coastal Carolinas. The elevated above-normal precipitation probabilties extend north to the western Corn Belt and also along the West Coast to Oregon given the good model agreement and strong/very strong El Nino composites. Excellent model consistency the past few months along with strong/very strong El Nino composites support below-normal precipitation probabilities exceeding 50% across the northern Rockies and much of Mainland Alaska. Consistent with the El Nino response and its southward shift in the storm track, elevated below-normal precipitation probabilities are forecast for parts of the Great Lakes and Northern Great Plains. The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) has remained negative throughout the 2020s. Although the October 2026 PDO value was negative, positive SST anomalies have diminished over the northeastern Pacific due to fall storminess. It is uncertain if the -PDO persists through the 2026-27 winter, and regardless, it is likely that the historically strong El Nino will be the major influence on the precipitation pattern across the Lower 48 states. El Nino impacts typically peak during the late winter across the Southeast, which supports maintaining large above-normal precipitation probabilities (> 70%) for that region through JFM. Since El Nino impacts are expected to linger into the spring, there is greater than a 40% chance of above-normal precipitation across much of California along with parts of the Southwest and Southeast during FMA and MAM. The precipitation outlooks from MJJ through OND 2027 are based on the ENSO-OCN forecast tool which is from the CPC SST consolidation (ENSO component) and long term temperature trends (Optimal Climate Normal). Historically, La Nina follows a strong El Nino and given this likelihood, the NDJ and DJF 2027-28 outlooks were based more on La Nina influences.
